header.author: Propertius, Sextus
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's phi0620.phi001.perseus-lat3, from the Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. Only some passages are translated so far: those that the Atlas of Ancient Myth, Magic in the Ancient Texts and the demons-and-angels study cite.

notes.4.1.69: 4.1.109: the text reads ‘it’ (‘goes’), which does not construe with the accusative ships of 110; translated by the evident sense, that Calchas freed the ships held fast at Aulis.
notes.4.5.3: 4.5.19–20 are corrupt (‘perure’ is not a Latin word) and do not construe; the rendering guesses at the sense, that steady coaxing wears down resistance.
notes.1.1.17: ‘Cytinaean’ (1.1.24) is an uncertain name; it probably means Colchian, i.e. Medea’s.

nodes.text: In my case slow Love devises no arts,
and does not remember to go by the familiar paths, as before.
But you, who have the trick of drawing down the moon
and the task of performing rites on magic hearths,
come now, turn the mind of my mistress,
and make her grow paler than my face!
Then I would believe that you can lead ghosts and stars
with Cytinaean spells.
Or you, friends, who too late call back one who has fallen,
seek aid for a heart that is not sane.
In vain was perfume poured on my hair,
and [in vain] my foot went lingering with measured step.
Here no herb avails, no Cytaean witch of the night,
no grasses cooked by Perimede’s hand;
for to what lying seer am I not a source of gain?
what old woman does not turn over my dreams ten times?
For where we see neither causes nor open blows,
the way by which so many ills nevertheless come is hidden;
this sick man needs no doctors, no soft beds,
no season of the sky or breeze harms him;
he walks about — and suddenly his friends marvel at his funeral!
So unforeseeable is whatever is called love.
Now, as best you can, wounded one, bow to fate:
both god and the hard day itself are turning.
The *rhombi* [magic wheels] whirled to the magic chant fail,
and the laurel lies scorched on the dead hearth;
and now the Moon refuses to come down from the sky so often,
and a black bird sings a deadly omen.
One boat of fate will carry our loves,
with dusky sail, to the lakes below.
Does he rejoice that I waste away alone in an empty bed?
If he likes, let him trample on my death, Lygdamus.
Not by her character but by herbs has that wicked woman beaten me:
he is drawn along by the threaded wheel of the *rhombus* [magic wheel].
Him the monstrous things of the toad swollen with venom
and bones gathered from dried-up snakes drag [to her],
and screech-owl feathers found among fallen tombs,
and a woollen fillet bound round a funeral bed.
If my dreams do not sing in vain, Lygdamus, I swear it,
punishment will lie before my feet, late but full;
I shall sing of rites and days and the ancient names of places:
towards these turning-posts my horse must sweat.
Where are you rushing, heedless, to tell fates, wandering Propertius?
The threads were not spun from a favourable distaff.
By singing you summon tears; Apollo is turned away:
you demand from an unwilling lyre words you will regret.
I will bring sure things from sure authorities, or I am a seer
who does not know how to move the signs on the bronze sphere.
Babylonian Orops, offspring of Archytas, begot me,
Horos, and my house is descended from my forefather Conon.
The gods are my witnesses that I have not disgraced my kin,
and that in my books nothing comes before good faith.
Now they have made a profit of the gods, and (by gold is deceived
Jupiter) of the repeated signs of the slanting wheel,
and the lucky stars of Jupiter and the rapacious ones of Mars,
and the star of Saturn, heavy on every head;
what the Fishes portend, and the bold sign of the Lion,
and Capricorn, bathed in the western water.
I shall say: “Troy, you will fall, and, Trojan Rome, you will rise again”;
and I shall sing of the long graves of sea and land.
I said, when Arria was sending out her twin sons
(she was giving her sons arms, though a god forbade):
that they could not bring their spears back to their fathers’ Penates;
and indeed two tombs now confirm my credit.
For Lupercus, while shielding his horse’s wounded face,
alas, took poor care of himself when the horse fell;
and Gallus, while guarding in camp the standards entrusted to him,
fell before the bloody beak of his eagle:
fated boys, two deaths for a greedy mother!
True, but against my will, that prophecy was borne out.
I too, when Lucina was drawing out Cinara’s pains,
and the slow burden of her womb was causing delay,
said: make a vow to Juno that will be granted;
she gave birth: the palm was awarded to my books!
This neither the sandy cave of Libyan Jove explains,
nor the entrail that speaks of the gods entrusted to it,
nor anyone who has noted the moving wings of a crow,
nor the shade of the dead that rises from magic waters:
you must watch the path of the sky, and through the stars the true
track, and seek certainty from the five zones.
Calchas will be a weighty example: for at Aulis he
[loosed] the ships that clung so well to the holy rocks;
and may your Manes find no rest on your ashes, and may avenging Cerberus
terrify your foul bones with hungry howling!
She was skilled to soften even Hippolytus as he refused Venus,
and was always the worst bird of omen for a harmonious bed;
even Penelope, ignoring the report of her husband,
she would force to marry lustful Antinous.
Should she wish it, the magnet will not be able to draw iron,
and a bird will be a stepmother to its own nestlings.
Indeed, if she brought Colline herbs to the trench,
solid things would melt away in running water:
bold to impose laws on the enchanted moon
and to disguise her body as a nocturnal wolf,
so that by cunning she might blind watchful husbands,
she dug out with her nail the innocent eyes of crows;
and she consulted screech owls about my blood, and against me
gathered *hippomanes*, the seed of a pregnant mare.
She would win her task with pleading words, as though coaxing … could burn through,
and busy wrongdoing cut a stony road:
